steps.title: Across the government, full releases fell from 41.6% to 9.5%

p: In the annual reports, every closed request ends in one of 12 ways. Four are drawn here, each as a share of all requests closed that year: released in full, partly released, no records found, and fully denied on exemptions. The other eight (such as referred, withdrawn or duplicate) stay in the total.
Released in full fell from 41.6% in FY2008 to 9.5% in FY2025.
Partly released rose from 17.8% to 37.7%. It has been the most common of the four in every year since FY2014; before that, released in full was.
No records found rose from 15.2% to 29.7%, with a dip in FY2018 (22.0% to 14.8%). Fully denied on exemptions stayed small: 3.8% to 3.2%.

The curve is uneven, and one government-wide line can combine very different agencies. Is this a pattern shared across agencies, or the work of a few agencies with many requests or unusual outcomes? We start with DHS, which closes a very large number of requests.

steps.method: Share = requests closed that way ÷ all requests closed that year. Government totals add up every agency's reported total. FY2008–09: 26 agencies are not yet in the foia.gov data.

charts.title: Share of all closed requests, all agencies

steps.title: DHS now closes 6 in 10 requests, and it rarely releases in full

p: The same figures, split into DHS and everyone else (“outside DHS”: every other agency and component).

DHS closed about 109,000 requests in FY2008, 18.9% of all. In FY2025 it closed about 995,000, more than 9 times as many and 60.8% of all. Outside DHS, closed requests grew only from about 469,000 to about 640,000. DHS has closed more than half of all requests every year since FY2020 (49.0% in FY2019).
In every year DHS released in full less often than the rest of the government: 11.4% in FY2008 and 2.4% in FY2025, never above 12.1%. Outside DHS the share fell from 48.7% to 20.7%.
The government-wide share is an average of DHS and outside DHS, weighted by how many requests each closes. Since DHS passed half, the government-wide line (grey, dashed) sits closer to DHS's.
So one national line can hide opposite movements. Partly released rose government-wide from 17.8% to 37.7%; outside DHS it rose from 10.0% to 34.3%, while at DHS it fell from 51.3% to 40.0%.

steps.method: Each share is out of that group's own closed requests. “Outside DHS” includes NARA and every other agency.

steps.title: A quarter to a half of the national drop comes from DHS handling more of the requests

p: The government-wide full-release share fell 32.1 points (41.6% to 9.5%). Two things changed at once: the rates (DHS 11.4% to 2.4%, outside DHS 48.7% to 20.7%) and DHS's share of closed requests (18.9% to 60.8%). How much of the fall is agencies releasing in full less often, and how much is more requests going to DHS, which rarely releases in full?

Change one thing at a time, as in the example with made-up numbers: first the rates with the request counts held fixed, then the counts with the rates held fixed. The middle row never happened; it only separates the two changes.

Done in the other order, the parts come out different. The method (a composition decomposition, Kitagawa 1955) takes the average of the two orders and reports both as a range. In either order the parts add up exactly to the total.
About 16.8 points come from the share outside DHS falling (10.9–22.7), about 11.7 from DHS handling more of the requests (7.7–15.7), and about 3.6 from DHS's own share falling (1.7–5.5).
So a quarter to a half of the national drop is the shift toward DHS. But outside DHS the share fell on its own: 10.9 to 22.7 points, whichever order is used.

Inside DHS there is a different change: its no-records share rose from 7.9% to 40.2% (most of the added count is at CBP and USCIS), while outside DHS it did not rise (16.9% to 13.4%). That is kept as a separate lead. The rest of this storyline follows the fall outside DHS: is it driven by individual agencies?

steps.method: An arithmetic split: it shows how many points each part accounts for, not why. It uses two groups only; step 8 splits by agency.

steps.title: NARA's outcomes swing from year to year, so it is set aside

p: Outside DHS, the full-release share jumps from 33.2% in FY2017 to 43.4% in FY2018. Most of that jump is one agency, the National Archives (NARA). The bars show how NARA's own requests ended each year.

NARA's most common outcome changes every few years: no records found in FY2008–17 (78% or more each year), released in full in FY2018–19 (68.1% and 71.6%), partly released in FY2020 (87.1%), released in full again in FY2021 (76.8%), and partly released in FY2022–25 (60.3%–82.4%).
NARA is 1.8%–15.2% of the requests closed outside DHS, enough to put swings into that line. Without NARA, the FY2017–18 jump is only 38.0% to 40.1%.

Mainly the middle years. The endpoints barely move: released in full goes from 48.7% to 20.7% with NARA and from 50.0% to 21.4% without it; the widest gap between the two lines is 5.2 points (FY2019). Setting NARA aside does not create the long-run fall.
The reports do not say why NARA's categories change, and we do not decide whether they are errors. NARA is set aside, not corrected; its pattern is a lead of its own.

steps.method: From here on, every figure is for agencies outside DHS and NARA, unless it says otherwise.

steps.title: Outside DHS and NARA, full releases fell from 50.0% to 21.4%

p: The same outcomes, now only for agencies outside DHS and NARA. The eight other ways a request can end (such as referred, withdrawn, duplicate or improper) are grouped as “other closures”, so the five lines add up to 100% every year.

Released in full fell from 50.0% in FY2008 to 21.4% in FY2025. Partly released rose from 10.2% to 32.3%. No records found barely moved (14.7% to 13.5%), and full denials on exemptions stayed low (4.6%–9.5% a year).

The fall is not every year. It is flat in FY2009–13 (45.5%–47.3%) and rises 2.1 points in FY2018, when two units that almost always release in full closed many more requests (USDA's FSA +2.51 points, DOJ's EOIR +1.51). FY2008 has the fewest agencies in the data; counted from FY2010 the fall is 47.0% to 21.4%.
Partly released rose 22.0 points, less than the 28.5-point fall. Other closures rose 6.3 points (20.5% to 26.8%): improper requests 3.7% to 8.4%, duplicates 1.9% to 4.3%, other reasons 1.5% to 3.9%.
So these are two shifts in yearly totals, not the same requests moving from full to partial release.
Partly released stays flat for years and then jumps from FY2023. Is that rise shared, or one unit?

steps.method: Shares of all requests closed outside DHS and NARA. The changes on the right are in percentage points and add up to zero.

steps.title: Since FY2017, the rise in partial releases is one component: VA's VBA

p: Partly released stayed at 21.2%–24.4% every year in FY2014–22, then jumped: 23.1% in FY2022, 27.9% in FY2023, 31.7% in FY2024 and 32.3% in FY2025. We split the jump by unit: each unit's partial releases as a share of all closed requests, later year minus FY2022. The parts add up exactly.
Almost all of it is the Veterans Benefits Administration (VBA), part of VA (table). Every other unit together pulled the other way.

VBA's volume and outcomes changed at the same time. It closed 7,586 requests in FY2022 and 99,224 in FY2025 (2.1% to 16.2% of all requests closed outside DHS and NARA), and its partly-released share went from 31.3% to 95.0% while its full-release share fell from 56.0% to 1.5%.

sections.h: The test: remove VBA from all years
p: Released in full still falls, from 48.6% to 25.3%, so VBA does not drive that decline.

Partly released has two periods. In FY2008–17 it still rises 12.3 points without VBA. In FY2017–25 it rises 9.0 points with VBA but falls 2.8 without it (22.9% to 20.1%). Of 571 single removals (step 9), only removing VBA or all of VA does this.

sections.h: What replaced full releases, without VBA
p: In FY2017–25, mostly other closures: +14.9 points (improper requests, other reasons, duplicates). The rise is spread across many units: the largest are DOJ's EOIR (+2.2) and HHS's CMS (+1.6); the top ten add +8.3 and all others +6.6.

steps.method: The reports do not say why VBA changed. We do not decide whether it changed how it handles requests or how it reports them.

steps.kicker: Outside DHS and NARA · without VBA
steps.title: Without VBA, most of the recent fall is requests closed without any records processed

p: A request whose records were reviewed must end as released in full, partly released or fully denied on exemptions. The other nine ways, including no records found, are used only when no records were processed.

So a falling full-release share can mean two things: less released in full among reviewed requests, or more requests closed without any records processed. The share splits exactly into two factors: (reviewed ÷ all closed) × (released in full ÷ reviewed).
Among reviewed requests, the full-release share also fell: outside DHS and NARA 77.2% (FY2008), 54.4% (FY2017) and 35.9% (FY2025); without VBA 76.0%, 54.7% and 48.1%.
FY2008–17, without VBA: the whole fall comes from less released among reviewed requests (−14.24 points); the reviewed share actually rose (64.0% to 69.6%).

FY2017–25, without VBA: the share fell 12.74 points. 8.74 of them come from the reviewed share falling (69.6% to 52.6%, more requests closed without records processed), and only 4.00 from less released among reviewed requests (54.7% to 48.1%).

sections.h: A fact that does not depend on the denominator
p: Without VBA, the number of full releases fell from 147,853 in FY2017 to 129,974 in FY2025, while closed requests rose from 388,535 to 513,446.

steps.method: Part 1 = change in the reviewed share × the two-year average of the other factor; part 2 = the rest, so the two parts add up exactly. Computed from two-decimal values, as in the notebook.

steps.kicker: Outside DHS and NARA · by agency
steps.title: The fall comes mostly from agencies' own shares, and most agencies fell

p: Step 3 split the national fall between DHS and the rest. Here the same split is done agency by agency outside DHS and NARA: did agencies' own full-release shares fall, or did requests shift toward agencies that release less in full?

Within-agency change = each agency's change in its own share × its weight (its share of all closed requests), added up. The rest is the remainder: shifts in weight, and agencies with data in only one of the two years.
FY2017–25: the share fell 16.57 points. The within-agency change is 13.13 to 13.85 points depending on which year's weights are used (13.49 on average), so most of the fall is agencies' own shares.

FY2008–17: the share fell 11.97 points; the within-agency change is 5.89 to 14.31 (10.10 on average). The range is wide because VA and HHS both fell and shrank (VA's weight 21.6% to 6.4%, HHS's 14.6% to 8.8%), and 26 agencies are missing from the FY2008 data.
FY2008–17 is concentrated in VA, HHS and SSA. FY2017–25 is broader: VA, DoW (DoD), DOT, DOJ, HHS and USDA all fell (charts, average weights).

FY2017–25: 87 of the 107 agencies with data in both years released in full less often (81%); among agencies with 1,000 or more closed requests, 24 of 26 (92%). The agencies that fell handled 96%–97% of these agencies' FY2025 requests, whatever the size cut-off. By component: 278 of 340 (82%).

DOJ's share rose over FY2008–25 (33.9% to 39.3%) although both its parts fell: EOIR 71.3% to 56.9%, the rest of DOJ 23.2% to 8.8%. EOIR, which releases in full often, grew from 22.2% to 63.3% of DOJ's requests. This is a Simpson's paradox: the total moves opposite to every part.

steps.method: Composition decomposition by agency (Kitagawa 1955), with start-year, end-year or average weights. Agency counts compare each agency's own share in the two years; an agency at the same share in both years is not counted as falling.

steps.title: Leave out any one of 571 agencies or components, and full releases still fall

p: Earlier steps followed oddities as they appeared (NARA, the FY2018 rise, VBA, EOIR). This step checks them all at once: remove one agency or one component from every year (571 removals: 126 agencies and 445 components; an agency with no components counts once) and recompute each period's change.

Released in full falls in every period under every removal. The smallest falls: −8.0 points in FY2008–17 (without HHS's CMS), −12.7 in FY2017–25 (without VBA), −23.1 over FY2008–25 (without all of VA). With FY2024 as the end year, it still falls at least 19.6 points.

Partly released: the FY2008–17 rise holds under every removal (at least +9.9 points). No records found: the FY2008–25 change stays between −2.9 and +1.0 points, nothing like the fall in full releases.

sections.h: One unit pulls the other way: EOIR
p: The biggest falls come from removing all of DOJ (−36.7 points) or its EOIR, the immigration courts (−34.3), both larger than the −28.5 with no removal. EOIR releases in full often and grew from 3.0% of requests closed outside DHS and NARA in FY2008 to 21.9% in FY2023, which props up the total. The FY2018 rise (EOIR +1.51 points) and a FY2023 rise when VBA is left out (EOIR +7.7) both came in years when EOIR's volume jumped.

Using only the 67 agencies with data in all 18 years: 50.0%, 37.5% and 20.7% in FY2008, FY2017 and FY2025, almost the same as 50.0%, 38.0% and 21.4% for all agencies. They hold 83.5%–90.6% of closed requests each year from FY2010. The changing list of agencies does not drive the finding.

steps.method: One unit removed at a time, from all years. VBA and EOIR were also removed together; other combinations of several units were not tested. These are descriptive checks, not causal identification.

steps.title: A shrinking share of requests is released in full

p: Outside DHS and NARA, full releases fell from 50.0% of closed requests in FY2008 to 21.4% in FY2025. The fall remains after removing any single agency or component, and it comes mainly from agencies' own full-release shares falling, not from a shift in which agencies handle requests.
Nationally the share fell 32.1 points; about 11.7 of them only reflect DHS closing more of the requests (step 3).
It falls in both periods: −12.0 points in FY2008–17 and −16.6 in FY2017–25, and at least 8.0 and 12.7 after any single removal (step 9).
Most agencies fell: in FY2017–25, 87 of 107 agencies released in full less often, and they handled 96%–97% of these agencies' requests (step 8).

What replaced full releases differs by period: partial releases in FY2008–17; in FY2017–25 the rise in partial releases is VBA, and without VBA most of the fall (8.74 of 12.74 points) is more requests closed without records processed (steps 6–7).
No records found did not rise with it: −1.2 points over FY2008–25 (step 5).
That the whole national decline is agencies releasing less: about 11.7 points reflect DHS's growing weight.
That partial releases have been rising lately, without mentioning VBA.
That the recent fall is all “agencies released less of what they reviewed”: without VBA, most of it is requests closed without records processed.
Any cause. The reports show that agencies' own shares fell, not whether request types, exemption use or reporting practice changed.

DHS's rising no-records share, mainly CBP and USCIS · NARA's swings between categories · VBA's switch to partial releases from FY2023 · EOIR's growing weight · the broad rise in other closures without VBA in FY2017–25.

steps.method: Annual totals reported by the agencies themselves; they do not follow individual requests or count pages released. 26 agencies are missing from the FY2008 data; FY2025 has no later report to compare with yet. Full analysis: Storyline 1 notebook.
